claims.text: The protective coating has a predominant FCC matrix containing finely dispersed, coherent BCC regions or precipitates.
Creep resistance is primarily governed by the coherency and fine dispersion of the secondary BCC phase in the FCC matrix.
Coherent BCC regions act as pinning sites that impede dislocation glide.
Coherent BCC regions restrict dislocation climb by limiting diffusion.
Reduced dislocation glide and climb lower steady-state creep strain under continuous loading.
FCC/BCC interfaces associated with a coherent, uniformly distributed BCC phase act as dislocation barriers.
Dislocations in the FCC matrix become mobile under sustained stress below the coating's yield limit.
The BCC regions locally reduce diffusion rates.
The combined obstruction of glide and inhibition of climb minimizes accumulated creep deformation.
A fine, coherent BCC dispersion will produce a lower steady-state creep strain rate than a coarse or incoherent BCC distribution.
A fine, coherent BCC dispersion will delay the onset of tertiary creep relative to a coarse or incoherent BCC distribution.
The proposed mechanism operates in an intermediate-temperature regime, exemplified as 500–700 °C, where diffusion is activated but remains slow.
At very high temperatures, diffusional creep or grain-boundary sliding may become significant.
At excessively high stresses, mechanisms other than coherent-BCC interfacial strengthening may become significant.
Grain size, interface chemistry, and secondary-phase transformations during long-term loading may affect creep behavior.
